intro.html: Most people lean one way or another: toward music or math, toward cats or dogs, toward sleeping late or rising early. This topic gives you ten words for those leanings, from natural talents to favorite treats to everyday habits.

Tendencies: inclination, propensity, proclivity (often a bad habit), predisposed (leaning that way before you start). Likings: affinity, penchant, predilection. Nature and talent: disposition (usual mood), aptitude (natural ability). Habit: wont.
Look for the pictures of leaning and hanging inside them: inclination and proclivity come from Latin words for leaning and sloping, and propensity and penchant from words for hanging.

words.ex: Dev has an {inclination} to doodle in the margins of every notebook.
words.ctx: Though her parents hoped she would study law, Rosa’s {inclination} was toward the sea; she spent every free hour on the docks, learning to sail.
words.etym: From Latin inclinare, “to lean toward”: in- (toward) + clinare (to bend).

mn.text: Every morning the sunflowers lean toward the sun, and so does Rosa, who heads straight for the sunny dock; leaning toward what you like is an {inclination}.

scene.alt: A girl and two sunflowers all lean toward the bright sun.

words.def: a person’s usual mood or nature
words.ex: Our mail carrier has a sunny {disposition}; she whistles even in the pouring rain.
words.ctx: The two puppies came from the same litter but had very different {dispositions}: one was calm and gentle, while the other barked at every leaf that moved.
words.etym: From Latin dispositio, “arrangement,” from disponere (to arrange): dis- (apart) + ponere (to place).

mn.cue: a SUNNY DISPOSITION: the weather inside you
mn.text: Even in a rainstorm, Nell whistles and smiles as if a little sun followed her around; her usual mood, her {disposition}, is sunny.

scene.alt: A cheerful woman walks under her own little sun while a grumpy man stands under a rain cloud.

words.def: a natural ability to learn or do something
words.ex: Maya showed an early {aptitude} for languages and spoke three by age ten.
words.ctx: Kai had never touched a piano before, but his {aptitude} was obvious: within a week he was playing songs by ear that took other students months to learn.
words.etym: From Late Latin aptitudo, “fitness,” from aptus (fit, suited).

mn.text: The very first time Kai sits at a piano, he plays a whole song by ear; he has an {aptitude} for music.

scene.alt: A boy plays the piano on his first try while a woman claps in amazement.

words.def: a natural liking for, or sense of connection with, someone or something
words.ex: Ivy has always had an {affinity} for animals; stray cats follow her home.
words.ctx: Though they had grown up on opposite sides of the world, the two cousins felt an instant {affinity}, finishing each other’s sentences within an hour of meeting.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

words.etym: From Latin affinitas, “closeness, relationship,” from affinis (bordering on, related): ad- (to) + finis (border).

mn.cue: a FIN-ITY: the girl and the whale
mn.text: Every time Ivy visits the harbor, the same friendly whale swims up and waves a fin at her; the two share a natural {affinity}.

scene.alt: A girl on a dock waves to a friendly whale that swims up beside her.

words.ex: Grandpa has a {penchant} for loud plaid shirts.
words.ctx: Her {penchant} for adventure showed early: by age ten she had climbed every tree on the block and tried to build a raft out of an old door.
words.etym: From French penchant, “leaning,” from pencher (to lean).

mn.cue: PEN-CHANT: she can never pass up a PEN
mn.text: Lin cannot walk past a stationery shop without buying one more pen; she has a {penchant} for pens.

scene.alt: A woman lovingly holds up a new pen beside a box overflowing with pens.

words.def: a natural tendency to act in a certain way
words.ex: Our puppy has a {propensity} for chewing shoes.
words.ctx: Given his {propensity} to exaggerate, nobody believed Jonah when he claimed to have seen a bear in the school parking lot.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

words.etym: From Latin propensus, “inclined,” from propendere (to hang forward): pro- (forward) + pendere (to hang).

mn.text: Leave a shoe by the door and Rufus will find it within a minute; the puppy has a {propensity} for chewing shoes.

scene.alt: A happy puppy chews a shoe among other chewed shoes while its owner scolds.

words.def: a tendency, often toward something one should not do
words.ex: The raccoon’s {proclivity} for raiding trash cans did not make it popular with the neighbors.
words.ctx: His {proclivity} for arguing with referees cost the team several penalties, and the coach finally benched him for the rest of the season.

roots.means: the state or quality of being

words.etym: From Latin proclivitas, from proclivis (sloping forward): pro- (forward) + clivus (slope).
words.note: Proclivity often hints at a bad habit; penchant and predilection are usually neutral or fond.

mn.text: No matter how many signs say NO CLIMBING, Pip always scrambles up the slide the wrong way; he has a {proclivity} for it.

scene.alt: A boy scrambles up a slide the wrong way past a sign that says no climbing.

words.ex: The cat has a {predilection} for napping in the laundry basket.
words.ctx: At the dessert table, Grandma revealed her {predilection} at once, skipping the cakes and pies and heading straight for the lemon bars.
words.etym: From Medieval Latin praedilectio, from praediligere (to prefer): prae- (before) + diligere (to love, to choose).

mn.text: At every party, Granny Mae walks right past the cakes and pies to the lemon bars; lemon is her {predilection}.

scene.alt: A grandmother walks past cakes and pies and reaches happily for a lemon treat.

words.def: inclined ahead of time to act or think a certain way
words.ex: Having grown up near the sea, Omar was {predisposed} to love sailing.
words.ctx: The judges were {predisposed} to favor the hometown team, so the visitors knew they would have to play twice as well to win.
words.etym: From pre- (before) + dispose (to incline, to arrange).

mn.cue: PRE-DISPOSED: leaning that way from the START
mn.text: Born into a family of bakers, little Theo seemed {predisposed} to love baking; his very first word was “Cake!”

scene.alt: A toddler in a chef’s hat says cake between his two baker parents.

words.def: a habit or usual way of acting
words.ex: As was his {wont}, Grandpa rose at dawn to feed the chickens.
words.ctx: Rather than rush to work, as was her {wont}, Ada strolled slowly through the park that morning, stopping to watch the ducks.
words.note: Wont is also an adjective: “he is wont to sing in the shower” means he usually does. Do not confuse it with won’t (will not).

mn.cue: WONT: what he always WANTS to do
mn.text: Every morning at six, as is his {wont}, Grandpa Gus feeds the chickens in his slippers.

scene.alt: A grandfather feeds his chickens at dawn, as he does every morning.

after.html: Wont (a habit, said WAWNT, like want in many American accents) is a different word from won’t (will not). “As is her wont” means “as she usually does.”

items.q: Which word most often hints at a bad habit?
items.why: Proclivity usually suggests a tendency toward something unwise. Aptitude is a talent; affinity and predilection are likings.

items.q: “As is her wont, Ada took the long way home.” This means Ada…
choices: refused to take the long way
items.why: Wont means habit: she does this as usual.

items.q: Which word means a natural ability, not just a liking?
items.why: Aptitude is a natural ability to learn or do something. The others are likings.

items.q: The root clin in inclination (and cliv in proclivity) means…
items.why: clinare means to bend or lean, and clivus means a slope: an inclination is a leaning.
